title: Given a rod of length N and a list of prices for each length, cut the rod into pieces to maximize total revenue, where each length can be used any number of times. Explain how this is an Unbounded Knapsack, the DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Rod Cutting (Maximize Revenue by Cutting a Rod into Pieces)

s1_definition.profdef: Rod Cutting is an Unbounded Knapsack problem where the capacity is the rod length, each cut length is an item with its length as weight and its price as value, and lengths may be reused. We fill a length-indexed DP sweeping low to high and the answer is the best revenue for the full length. Time is N squared in the common formulation and space is N.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India holds a fixed-term deposit of a certain duration and can break it into sub-terms, each sub-term paying a known rate. The bank wants to split the term to maximize total interest, reusing profitable sub-terms as often as they fit. Rod Cutting maximizes that total.
s1_definition.oneliner: Lengths are unlimited-use items; maximize revenue for the full length with an upward DP sweep.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rod Cutting is an Unbounded Knapsack problem where the capacity is the rod length, each cut length is an item with its length as weight and its price as value, and lengths may be reused. We fill a length-indexed DP sweeping low to high and the answer is the best revenue for the full length. Time is N squared in the common formulation and space is N.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India holds a fixed-term deposit of a certain duration and can break it into sub-terms, each sub-term paying a known rate. The bank wants to split the term to maximize total interest, reusing profitable sub-terms as often as they fit. Rod Cutting maximizes that total.

**One line to remember:** Lengths are unlimited-use items; maximize revenue for the full length with an upward DP sweep.

sections.s2_technical:
We model each available length `len` with price `price[len]` as an item whose weight is `len` and whose value is `price[len]`. Because any length can be cut repeatedly, this is Unbounded Knapsack with capacity equal to the rod length N.

The one-dimensional DP is `dp[0] = 0`, and for each length `len` we sweep capacity from `len` up to N with `dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], price[len] + dp[c - len])`. The upward sweep lets us reuse the same length many times, so a rod can be cut into several identical profitable pieces. A concrete step: if length three sells for nine and we are at total length six, `dp[6]` can build on `dp[3]` that already used a length-three piece, giving two such pieces. Senior nuance: the answer is `dp[N]`, and reconstructing the actual cuts needs a parallel record of which length improved each capacity, which is useful when the business wants the cut plan, not just the revenue.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India holds a fixed-term deposit of a whole-number duration and can split it into sub-terms, each sub-term paying a published interest amount for that length. The treasury team wants to split the full term to maximize total interest, and the same profitable sub-term length can be reused as many times as it fits. This is exactly how Rod Cutting works: it is Unbounded Knapsack over lengths.

The code defines a `TermSplitService` exposing `maxRevenue(prices, length)` where `prices[i]` is the interest for a sub-term of length `i`, returning the best total interest. A `Demo` runs it over a price list and a term length and logs the maximum interest.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is prices for lengths one through four of 1, 5, 8, 9 and a full term length of four. The dp array spans zero through four, all zero to start.

Step 1 — Process length one, price one. Sweeping one up to four, each dp[c] becomes c because c pieces of length one each pay one. Now dp is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

Step 2 — Process length two, price five. Sweeping two up to four, dp[2] becomes max of 2 and 5 plus dp[0] equals 5; dp[3] becomes max of 3 and 5 plus dp[1] equals 6; dp[4] becomes max of 4 and 5 plus dp[2] which is 5 plus 5 equals 10. Now dp is 0, 1, 5, 6, 10.

Step 3 — Process length three, price eight. Sweeping three up to four, dp[3] becomes max of 6 and 8 plus dp[0] equals 8; dp[4] becomes max of 10 and 8 plus dp[1] equals 9, so stays 10. Now dp is 0, 1, 5, 8, 10.

Step 4 — Process length four, price nine. dp[4] becomes max of 10 and 9 plus dp[0] equals 9, so stays 10.

Step 5 — The best interest for a term of length four is dp[4], which is ten, achieved by two sub-terms of length two paying five each. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:14:20 PM com.bank.term.service.TermSplitService maxRevenue
INFO: Max interest for term 4 = 10
Oct 27, 2026 9:14:20 PM com.bank.term.TermSplitApplication main
INFO: Best total interest for a term of length 4: 10
```

```
  Input: prices[1..4] = [1,5,8,9], term length 4
    │
    ▼
  dp[0..4] initialized to 0
    │
    ▼
  For each length, sweep capacity LOW → HIGH
    │ len1 (p1): dp = 0 1 2 3 4
    │ len2 (p5): dp = 0 1 5 6 10
    │ len3 (p8): dp = 0 1 5 8 10
    │ len4 (p9): dp = 0 1 5 8 10
    ▼
  Answer dp[4] = 10  (two length-2 pieces)
  Output: best interest = 10
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rod Cutting is an Unbounded Knapsack problem once I map each available length to an item whose weight is that length and whose value is its price, with the rod length playing the role of capacity. Because any length can be cut as many times as it fits, the item is reusable, which is the defining feature of the unbounded pattern.

I fill a length-indexed array where each entry is the best revenue achievable for that total length. For each available length I sweep the capacity from that length up to the full length, taking the better of the current best or the price of this length plus the best revenue for the remaining length. The upward sweep is what lets the same profitable length appear several times in one rod, so the rod can be cut into multiple identical pieces when that maximizes revenue. The answer sits at the full length, and if the business needs the actual cut plan I keep a parallel record of which length improved each capacity.

At the National Bank of India I used this to split a fixed-term deposit into sub-terms, each paying a published interest for its length, to maximize total interest, reusing the most profitable sub-term length as often as it fit. I ran the length-indexed unbounded DP and read the answer at the full term. Explaining the mapping from lengths to reusable items, the upward sweep that enables repetition, and how to reconstruct the cuts is what shows an interviewer that I recognise Rod Cutting as a direct instance of Unbounded Knapsack.
